A: Context panel is empty by default ('Select an alert...') - roughly a quarter of the 1600x1000 viewport is dead space, and at full page the entire right column runs empty; asset/client context costs a click before it exists
The 24h trend chart occupies the prime position above the triage queue, so at 1000px only ~7 queue rows are visible; the queue is not visually the primary region
Chart's last x-axis label clipped ('16:0'); visible grey nested scrollbar strips between queue and context panel
40-client rail requires long scrolling with no compact fleet overview
B: At a tall 1600x2200 viewport the app-height layout leaves a large empty background band below the content (benign at the designed ~1000px height)
Client-estate grid uses cryptic 3-letter org codes with counts; needs hover/learning to decode
Bottom visible queue row clips mid-row at 1000px (scrollable region, minor)
Queue caps at 25 shown of 214 open (last 4h window) - defensible but the cut is only explained in a small header note

notes: B passes the 3-second test cleanly: the queue is the unambiguous primary region, the top critical alert is pre-selected with full asset/client context (crown-jewel tag, owner, open-alert counts, runbook), and SOC-native metrics (unacked, median time-to-ack, SLA at risk, telemetry coverage, stale/silent feed states with 'no data != no threat') show deeper domain reasoning visibly executed. A is handsome and well-engineered (validated severity palette, shape glyphs, chart table fallback, 40-client rail) but ships its default state with an empty context panel wasting a quarter of the screen and places the trend chart above the queue, burying the primary triage surface. Both are fully self-contained with working filters/actions; B adds a verified j/k/a/e keyboard flow and undo, which matters for repeated triage.
